prompt: Exact search over 100 million vectors of 1,024 numbers each. About how many multiply-adds per question, in billions?
G6: the right passage (24 hours) was retrieved, but the bot said 48 hours. What kind of miss, and what fixes it?

options.A: An answer miss: fix the prompt or the model, since a bigger k can't help
options.B: A grading miss: the judge misread an answer that was correct
options.C: A chunking miss: add overlap so the passage keeps its subject
options.D: A retrieval miss: raise k so that more of the ranked passages reach the prompt

prompt: Same ranks: 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1. What is recall@1, in percent?
What does half overlap between chunks fix?

options.A: A fact cut at a chunk boundary also appears whole in the neighbouring chunk
options.B: Fewer chunks need storing, because overlapping chunks are merged into one
options.C: The question and the chunks can now use two different embedding models
options.D: Large chunks mix fewer topics, because overlap removes their repeated words

prompt: Reference: “100 requests per minute per API key”. Why does exact match fail “100 requests per minute.”?

options.A: It compares meanings, and the final period changes the meaning
options.B: It applies the judge's rubric, which requires the words API key
options.C: It compares strings, so a right answer worded differently fails
options.D: It fails any answer shorter than the reference, right or wrong

prompt: In vector search, what is embedded ahead of time, and what at ask time?

options.A: The question ahead of time; every chunk at ask time, to stay fresh
options.B: Nothing ahead of time; the model embeds the docs during its prefill
options.C: Both at ask time, because each chunk's vector depends on the question
options.D: Every chunk ahead of time (the index); the question at ask time

prompt: Putting passage C2 in the prompt made “100” jump to 96%. What changed inside the model?

options.A: The weights updated to store the new fact, so later questions without C2 also answer 100
options.B: Nothing in the weights: attention read “100” from the passage now in the context
options.C: Temperature dropped, because a passage in the prompt makes sampling greedy
options.D: The vocabulary gained a token for 100, so the model could finally output it

prompt: “How often can I call search per minute?” Which method on its own matches “call” to “requests”?

options.A: Vector search, because similar meanings get similar embeddings
options.B: Keyword search, because rarer words count more in its scoring
options.C: Neither one, because only an LLM judge can match two synonyms
options.D: Keyword search, because both words appear somewhere in the docs

prompt: You raise the floor to 0.90. For the /search question, the best passage scores 0.86. What happens?

options.A: Nothing changes, because the floor only applies to off-topic questions
options.B: Every passage is dropped, so an answerable question gets “not in the docs”
options.C: Only C2 passes, because a high floor removes near-duplicate passages such as C3
options.D: The bot answers 10, because C3 is the one passage above the floor

prompt: How should you choose the score floor's value?

options.A: Set it to 0, because the model ignores irrelevant passages in the prompt anyway
options.B: Set it to the highest score seen, so only the very best passage ever passes
options.C: Tune it on test questions, including some whose right answer is “not in the docs”
options.D: Use 0.50 always, because cosine values are the same across embedding models

prompt: Why keep a golden set instead of trying a few questions by hand after each change?

options.A: Hand checks rely on the LLM judge, which disagrees with human labels far too often
options.B: The similarity score already shows whether an answer is right, so hand checks add nothing
options.C: A golden set makes retrieval itself faster, because the right answers get cached
options.D: The same questions with known answers every run, so scores compare and regressions show

prompt: What does computing recall@k need?

options.A: For each question, which passage is right and where it ranked
options.B: A person reading and grading every single answer the bot writes
options.C: The model's probability for every token of each answer
options.D: An LLM judge scoring each answer against a written rubric

prompt: In RAG, what does the generate stage actually receive?

options.A: The passages' embedding vectors, written into the model's weights for the length of one request
options.B: Only the question, because retrieval runs after generation to check the answer
options.C: A prompt with instructions, the top k retrieved passages as text, and the question
options.D: The whole docs index, which the model searches itself during its forward pass

prompt: How do you know an LLM judge can be trusted?

options.A: Measure its agreement with human labels on a sample; fix the rubric until it's high
options.B: Check that it passes longer, more detailed answers more often than short ones
options.C: It is a model too, so its grades are as accurate as the answers it is grading
options.D: Run it twice on the same answers; if both sets of grades match, the grades are correct

prompt: You paste 50,000 tokens of docs into every question, at $3 per million input tokens. What does one question cost, in dollars?
Why must the question and the chunks go through the same embedding model?

options.A: The context window only accepts vectors made by the model that writes the answer
options.B: Different models cut the docs into different chunks, so their ranks can't be compared
options.C: Keyword scores are computed from the embedding model's vocabulary of rare words
options.D: Vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces, so their cosine means nothing

prompt: An approximate index checks only the regions nearest the question. What does it give up for the speed?

options.A: Cost: every approximate search adds extra input tokens to the prompt
options.B: Freshness: a newly added vector can't be found until the next full rebuild
options.C: Recall: a true nearest neighbour in an unchecked region can be missed
options.D: Precision: the cosine scores it returns are rounded, so ties appear

prompt: With k = 1 the bot answered “10” from C3, which really says 10. Is that answer faithful, and is it right?

options.A: Faithful but wrong: it stuck to its passage, but retrieval sent the wrong one
options.B: Unfaithful but right: the model corrected a mistake in the passage
options.C: Unfaithful and wrong: it changed the number given in the passage it read
options.D: Faithful and right: it cited the passage it was given, so it is correct

prompt: “What does E1042 mean?” Vector search ranks the 429 passage first. Why does keyword search find C6?

options.A: Only C6 contains the exact token E1042, a rare word that keyword scoring rewards
options.B: Keyword search gives E1042 a longer vector, so its cosine with C6 comes out higher
options.C: Keyword search ranks passages by their length, and C6 is the shortest passage
options.D: Keyword search knows E1042 is an error code, so it ranks error passages first

prompt: Each question sends 100 tokens of instructions and question, plus k passages of 300 tokens. How many input tokens at k = 2?
Why is fine-tuning a poor way to add facts the bot must quote exactly?

options.A: Fine-tuning erases the model's earlier training, so it forgets how to write sentences
options.B: Fine-tuning only changes the tokenizer, so the new facts never reach the weights
options.C: Each edit needs a training run, and the model can't point to where a fact came from
options.D: A fine-tuned model needs a longer context window for every question it is asked

prompt: Right-passage ranks for six golden questions are 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1. What is recall@2, in percent?
Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1/(60 + rank) from each list. A passage is rank 2 in vector search and rank 1 in keyword search. What is its hybrid score?
Today: vector search, k = 3, recall 100%, 1,000 tokens per question. Gate: recall ≥ today and tokens ≤ today. Which change ships?

options.A: Vector search with k = 2: recall 83% with 700 tokens
options.B: Hybrid search with k = 1: recall 83% with 400 tokens
options.C: Hybrid search with k = 2: recall 100% with 700 tokens
options.D: Vector search with k = 4: recall 100% with 1,300 tokens

prompt: Your docs are 2M tokens and edited daily. Which approach fits?

options.A: RAG: about 1,000 input tokens per question, and edits show up once changed chunks are re-embedded
options.B: Long context: paste everything, because a bigger prompt always gives the model more facts to use
options.C: Raise k until it covers every chunk, because recall@k reaches 100% only when all chunks are sent
options.D: Fine-tuning: retrain daily, because the weights are the most reliable place to keep exact facts

prompt: Plain prompt, k = 1 → k = 3 on the golden set. Select all that are true.

options.A: End-to-end accuracy reaches 100%
options.B: Right answers rise from 2 to 5
options.C: G6's answer miss disappears
options.D: Retrieval misses drop from 3 to 0

prompt: With k = 1 the bot answered “10 requests per minute [C3]” to “How often can I call search per minute?”. Where was the bug?

options.A: Generation: the model had C2 in its prompt but copied the wrong number out of that same passage
options.B: Chunking: C2 was split at a boundary, so the number 100 was missing from every chunk sent
options.C: Retrieval: C3 (/upload) ranked above C2, so the model answered faithfully from the wrong passage
options.D: The model: it ignored the passage it was given and answered from its training data instead

prompt: The plain LLM judge passed “Limits vary by endpoint and plan; check your dashboard…”. What made it match the human label?

options.A: A rubric that says passing means stating 100 requests per minute for /search
options.B: Raising k, so that the judge sees more of the retrieved passages
options.C: A bigger judge model, because only small judges show verbosity bias
options.D: Switching to exact match, because exact match never passes long answers

prompt: Cosine similarity between a question and a passage measures…

options.A: How long the passage is compared with the length of the question
options.B: How likely the model is to generate the passage as its next text
options.C: How many exact words the question and the passage have in common
options.D: How closely their embedding vectors point in the same direction

prompt: Hybrid search raises recall@1 from 50% to 83%. Why still read the per-question list?

options.A: Hybrid scores use a different scale, so the two recall percentages don't compare
options.B: Recall@1 is computed per question, so the aggregate is always wrong
options.C: The golden set's questions change whenever the search method changes
options.D: An aggregate can hide a regression: G2 fell from #1 to #2 under hybrid

prompt: You raise k from 1 to 3 for the /search question. Select all that are true.

options.A: The model's weights now include the extra passages
options.B: Each question sends more input tokens, so it costs more
options.C: The right passage is more likely to be in the prompt
options.D: The model gets more unrelated text it has to ignore
options.E: Retrieval gets faster, because fewer passages are ranked

prompt: “Do you support GraphQL?” is not in the docs. With no score floor, what does the bot do?

options.A: Fails with an error, because the prompt then has no passage it is able to cite
options.B: Says it's not in the docs, because cosine is negative for every unrelated passage
options.C: Answers from the nearest passages anyway, because top-k always returns k results
options.D: Returns no passages, because vector search only ever returns exact word matches

prompt: You ask a model, with no docs in the prompt, for your API's /search limit (100 per minute, written only in your private docs). What does it most likely do?

options.A: Returns an error message, because it looks the fact up in its weights and finds no entry for it
options.B: Answers 100, because training on many similar API docs placed your exact limit in its weights
options.C: Asks for your docs, because a model can always tell which facts it never saw in training
options.D: Writes a plausible number, because no weights hold your limit and sampling still picks a token

prompt: In the regions toy, the question sits near a region border. Checking 1 of 16 regions finds only 1 of the 5 true nearest. Why?

options.A: Some true neighbours sit in nearby regions that weren't checked
options.B: The question's vector moves when fewer regions are being checked
options.C: One region holds fewer than 5 vectors, so it can't return 5 results
options.D: Inside each region, the index ranks vectors by keyword score instead

prompt: Why is one very large chunk (the whole page) a problem too?

options.A: Keyword search stops working, because large chunks contain no rare words
options.B: The model can't read chunks longer than one sentence, so they get skipped
options.C: Its one vector blends every topic, and each retrieval sends all of that text
options.D: Large chunks split facts more often, because their boundaries fall in the middle of words

prompt: Chunks of 6 words, no overlap: the chunk holding “100” reads “100 requests per minute per API”. Why is that a problem?

options.A: It is too long: six words is more than one embedding vector can hold for retrieval
options.B: It lost its subject: no chunk has /search with 100, so a /search question can't match it
options.C: It costs too much: small chunks send more tokens per question than large chunks do
options.D: It breaks the index: chunks must share some words, or the index refuses to store them

prompt: Your docs are 50K tokens and change rarely. The context window is 128K. What's the simplest good choice?

options.A: Paste all the docs into the prompt; prompt caching cuts the repeated cost
options.B: Fine-tune on the docs, because facts in the weights cost no input tokens
options.C: None works, because 50K tokens is over the model's context window limit
options.D: Build RAG, because a long prompt can never show which passage it used
